title: Mastering Convexity! - Systematic Investor 333
speakers: Richard Brennan (trend follower, East Coast Capital Management)
summary: Brennan presents convexity (Dave Dredge) as the core of trend following: Sharpe-world risk measures are flawed; small losses, anti-martingale pyramiding, and wide diversification harvest outliers. Kaastrup adds January 2025 dispersion data and cautions on open equity.

coverage.note: Nvidia drop, Global Alts conference, central bank divergence
trend vs mean reversion curves, convex vs concave
brakes analogy, adverse vs beneficial volatility, racetrack
uncertainty drives material events, barbell, linear illusion
convexity by horizon, options cost, trend diversity
flawed assumptions, low vol fragility, VaR contagion
shifting distribution, concave drag, risk as permanent loss
drawdown length, VaR, trend barbell, core capital
open equity risk for new investors, thousands of trades

completeness_estimate: 0.88 - first reader captured nearly all of Rich's convexity argument and Niels' data and interjections; missed the Niels/Asness risk-definition pushback, Rich's reply on closed-equity AUM and long-haul philosophy, option-hedge precision, linearity assumption, infinite yield and diversification-as-safety-net, and merged two speakers in the open-equity claim.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: financial markets are defined by convexity where small changes can lead to disproportionately large outcomes
claims.claim: Markets are non-linear: long muted regimes alternate with explosive moves and large drawdowns, so average volatility is a poor description of risk.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: Risk is being able to adapt to the market that's currently in play.
claims.claim: Risk should be managed by adapting to the current regime, not by an average volatility assumption.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we embrace convexity at all levels, not just in protection, but also in looking for opportunities through diversification and by attacking what we call these outliers
claims.claim: Trend following uses convexity for opportunity capture (diversification, outlier hunting) as well as protection, unlike tail-protection funds.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we don't expect that model to perform and so equity curves should expect drawdowns or what we call stagnation
claims.claim: Trend following earns nothing in trendless periods (stagnation) and rises sharply in trends, giving a non-linear payoff.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: when we are applying something like a mean reversion strategy or strategy with what we call negative skewed, we get a concave relationship
claims.claim: Mean reversion and negative-skew strategies yield many small wins then sudden large losses when an unpredicted regime hits (concave payoff).

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: convexity, which is effectively positive skew, it ensures that favorable volatility accelerates gains while we mitigate loss losses through effective risk management
claims.claim: Convexity equals positive skew: amplify gains when volatility is favorable and cap losses with risk management.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: convexity is about acceleration when conditions are favorable and braking effectively when conditions are not favorable
claims.claim: Convex process accelerates in favorable regimes and brakes (stops, small bets) in adverse regimes, rather than assuming constant conditions.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we don't treat all volatility as the same. There is adverse volatility, and there is beneficial volatility.
claims.claim: Volatility splits into adverse and beneficial; smoothing funds only limit adverse volatility and forgo upside.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we can achieve a higher compounded return if we exploit upside volatility
claims.claim: Exploiting upside volatility with good brakes gives higher compounded return than optimising for average speed, as an F1 car with brakes wins the lap.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: you're always going to be blindsided by these events that have never occurred in historical record like the COVID pandemic
claims.claim: Using history to set expected returns blindsides investors, because the most material events arise from uncertainty absent from the sample.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: the left side of the barbell is keeping our losses as small as possible, as linear as possible.
claims.claim: Barbell: keep losses small and linear on one side and amplify opportunity on the other, forcing asymmetry.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: these linear equity curves we often see put out by portfolio managers, they're actually the great illusion
claims.claim: Smooth linear equity curves reflect a temporary predictable environment and later become concave.
claims.testable: partly: look at smooth-curve fund blow-ups

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: The calamity occurs when suddenly the regime shifts with high leverage
claims.claim: Strategies that lever up predictable returns (LTCM, mean reversion, pattern recognition) fail at regime shift.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we have had stocks that are uncorrelated with bonds
claims.claim: The 60/40 portfolio rested on a negative or zero stock-bond correlation which turned positive, leaving it with no brakes.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: What blindsides the traditional investment community is things that they never expected or never saw in their detailed historical data sets
claims.claim: Models trained on history collapse in unprecedented environments; a backtest surviving does not ensure future survival.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: typically someone like Dave Dredge or whatever, they'll employ options to provide that degree of protection for a traditional portfolio
claims.claim: Tail protection funds add options to long-only portfolios to cover unforeseen collapses.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: even in with within our industry people might claim that oh, but trend followers are less provide less positive skew, less convexity today than they used to do
claims.claim: Convexity depends on horizon; short-term managers and tail funds claim to offer more convexity, and trend followers' skew has reportedly declined.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: There is no cost for our long short models in our trend following world, but we provide convexity at no cost.
claims.claim: Options protection costs premium (expiry worthless); trend following provides convexity without explicit premium, though with whipsaws.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we do have a degree of exposure and risk in relation to short-term adverse movements because our models can't respond quickly enough to their short-term movements
claims.claim: Medium-to-long-term trend models are exposed to sudden short-term shocks that options hedge immediately.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: trend following offers better, more diverse opportunities in its ability to exploit opportunities
claims.claim: Trend following covers far more markets than options, giving diversified outlier exposure.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: having things like trend following in the portfolio will not necessarily completely alleviate the issue, but it will certainly reduce some of the pain
claims.claim: Trend following in a multi-asset portfolio cushions events nobody imagined, so ask what you are doing about what you are not worried about.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: one of the greatest misconceptions is the belief that risk equates to volatility
claims.claim: Sharpe, standard deviation and VaR fail because crises (1987, 2002, 2008, COVID) come from unforeseen events; risk is not volatility.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: One is risk can be quantified using historical data. Two, markets behave in a linear fashion following normal distributions. Three, correlations persist into the future.
claims.claim: Five flawed assumptions of traditional finance: historical risk, normality, persistent correlations, estimable returns, all volatility bad.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: risk is a possibility distribution, not a probability distribution
claims.claim: Taleb: risk is about possible outcomes, not probabilities from the past.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: low volatility environments encourage excessive leverage, and they make markets more fragile and vulnerable to shocks
claims.claim: Long calm periods raise fragility (avalanche, flood, forest fire analogies), so low volatility is not safe.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: So, the assessment of VAR is going to totally underestimate the calamity.
claims.claim: VaR misses contagion because markets are connected complex adaptive systems.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: This is why risk cannot be managed exclusively through predictive models. It must be built into portfolio design.
claims.claim: Risk must be built into portfolio design (convexity), not only forecasted.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we're shifting the distribution to the right. So, we've got lots of small losses, but occasional massive wins
claims.claim: Positive skew optimises long-term compounded wealth.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: creates significant compounding drag and totally dilutes the compounding effect
claims.claim: Concave strategies with rare crippling losses cause compounding drag.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: Risk to me is permanent loss of capital.
claims.claim: Risk should be defined as permanent loss of capital, not volatility.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: In a trend following world, hardly any. Why? Because they apply positive convexity.
claims.claim: Few trend followers ever blow up whereas mean-reversion strategies (LTCM) do; no validated 20-30 year records exist for other styles.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the length of drawdown can be much more damaging to our psychology than actually a quick large drawdown
claims.claim: Long drawdowns hurt investor psychology more than deep short ones (Asness).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the possibilities as well as the probabilities of something crazy happening is probably higher today than ever before
claims.claim: The range and probability of extreme events is judged higher now.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's probably still a decent measure compared to some of the other ones
claims.claim: Correlation-aware VaR, used properly, remains a decent risk measure, better than Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: our ability to cut losses short at all times and let profits run
claims.claim: Trend following is a barbell of small losses and let profits run, with very small bet sizes.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we're only exploiting a very small risk bet of our core capital to our trade
claims.claim: Risk each trade as a small fraction of closed-trade core capital, letting unrealised equity run.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: with some managers the open trade equity became so large that people who bought into those funds at a certain time had open trade equity of 50, 60, 70%
claims.claim: Large open profits expose new investors to 50 percent drawdowns; allocate AUM on closed equity.

correction.issue: Two speakers merged: Niels only raises the risk (new investors holding funds with 50-70% open trade equity face large drawdowns, and the principle suits one's own money with an infinite runway). The suggestion to allocate AUM on closed equity is Rich's reply, not Niels's.
correction.fix: Niels: in funds whose open trade equity grew to 50-70% of NAV, new investors are exposed to a straight 50% drawdown that long-standing investors are not, so closed-equity sizing mainly suits own money; Rich replied separately that new AUM can be allocated on closed equity.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: Look at the the last 2,000 trades. Look at the last 4,000 trades.
claims.claim: Trend following should be judged on thousands of trades, not individual outcomes.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: trend following is really aggressively looking to amplify upside
claims.claim: Trend following amplifies upside by letting profits run and concentrating in material trends.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: and if it continues to go my way, I what we call apply an anti-martingale degree of progression into it
claims.claim: Take a small initial trade, add as it succeeds (anti-martingale) with an ensemble, for positive convexity.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: That is a concave strategy. That is a Martingale approach.
claims.claim: Martingale doubling after losses is concave: small gains but catastrophic risk.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: we're doing it to find those outliers wherever they may roam because these things are unpredictable
claims.claim: Wide diversification is for finding outliers since their location cannot be forecast.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: So, these single outlier events, they can offset dozens of small losses.
claims.claim: Ride winners until trends exhaust; one outlier (cocoa, equity rally) pays for dozens of small losses.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: Stops themselves can be broken. We know that in very fast-moving markets, they're not always observed
claims.claim: Small position size is the ultimate stop since stop orders can gap.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: you're required to have skin in the game for a very long period of time to exploit the power of the exponential growth that compounding gives
claims.claim: Survival through small bets keeps capital in play for compounding.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: people think they might be diversified, but in reality they're full of short ball strategies essentially
claims.claim: Investors who think they are diversified hold hidden short volatility exposure; a more divergent world favours trend.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: most traditional portfolios assume linearity. They're looking for the straightest possible um equity curve, the most linear equity curve, the curve with the highest Sharpe ratio
claims.claim: Traditional portfolio construction assumes a linear input-output world and so targets the straightest equity curve with the highest Sharpe ratio, which is inconsistent with non-linear markets where payoff shape matters more than smoothness.
claims.testable: partly - compare Sharpe-optimised vs skew-optimised portfolios

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's too much bleed. It's too expensive to provide convexity on a daily basis because it doesn't matter uh in the long run
claims.claim: Counter-view on convexity horizon: longer-term managers can argue that supplying convexity at short horizons (daily) costs too much bleed and does not matter for long-run results, so convexity should be defined by time frame (Quantica has a paper on this).
claims.testable: yes - compare cost of short-horizon convexity with long-run payoff

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: options is probably the purest way to get um protection for a traditional portfolio for adverse risk events because you can align the option exposure to what you're trying to protect
claims.claim: Options are the most precise hedge for a traditional portfolio because they can be matched to the specific risk (correlation risk, market risk), whereas trend following is a less targeted, free-of-premium form of convexity.
claims.testable: partly - hedge effectiveness vs cost testable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I mean, how many strategies in our careers have we really seen blow up completely?
claims.claim: Niels, citing Asness, pushes back that complete permanent loss of capital is rare in any strategy, so defining risk only that way is too narrow; he wants something in between because volatility can still feel like risk even if it is not the same.

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: you could apply a process that applies it based on closed equity. Um the unrealized equity is not a problem with the new incoming investor.
claims.claim: Rich's answer to the new-investor problem: allocate new AUM using closed equity, so open (unrealised) equity stays with existing investors and is not a new investor's problem; there are different models for this.
claims.indicator: closed equity vs open equity for AUM allocation
claims.conditions: funds with large open trade equity from a few trades
claims.testable: partly - simulate new-investor drawdown under both bases

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: do not do trend following unless you're prepared to do it for the long haul
claims.claim: The philosophy of trend following is long-horizon compounding with patience; using it for other purposes (as an allocation inside traditional portfolios, or managing outside AUM) adds concerns, which Rich calls the business of trend following as distinct from trend following itself.
claims.conditions: investors who cannot tolerate long drawdowns

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: the principle there is a return that pays for all of the costs you've had over the course of time
claims.claim: Rich's aim is 'infinite yield': an open-ended payoff from letting profits run so that one trend pays for all accumulated costs of small controlled losses, which are the price of staying in the game for the next unknown opportunity.
claims.conditions: requires patience and survival through losing streaks
claims.testable: yes - profit factor of top trades vs cumulative losses

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: is diversification as safety net. It's not only about a safety net, but it's also about spreading that net wide to capture those outliers, expanding the opportunity set, and also risk reduction through diversity.
claims.claim: Diversification in trend following serves three purposes: lower portfolio correlation and risk through diversity, a wider opportunity set, and capturing outliers wherever they appear.
claims.testable: yes - market count vs trend capture and risk
